item.title: Handing Change Points to an Agent - Precision and Latency in Production Monitoring Need Not Be a Trade-off
item.description:
A rule of thumb long circulated in operations is that about 70% of production incidents are caused by changes to a running system – binary releases, configuration pushes, feature flag switches. Given that, concentrating monitoring resources near those change points should in theory contain the impact of most regressions at minimal cost. Yet in engineering this is widely acknowledged as hard: not that nobody can write an alert, but that it is very hard to be both “accurate” and “early”, and harder still to make it run by itself inside an organisation.

Large-model agents are changing that equation. What deserves attention is not the concept of “AI operations” but a specific engineering shape: let the model read code and write monitoring specs, let deterministic programs execute the specs, and let the model investigate the monitoring items that fire. This structure can already find regressions in systems it knows nothing about at prototype stage, with better precision and latency than a year ago.

Why Change-Point Monitoring Has Always Been Hard to Land

First, see where the old approach got stuck. Change-point monitoring is not a technical problem but the “takeoff” problem of platform engineering, and it has three typical dilemmas.

The first is picking the wrong first users. The natural move is to pilot with the teams that have the best operations foundation and the strongest motivation. But those teams’ releases are already relatively safe, so the platform does not actually raise the overall operations water level; the value it offers is mainly toil reduction, a nice-to-have rather than a first-order safety improvement. Worse, precision is easy to achieve with such teams, so the new system ends up competing with existing alerts on recall and latency, with little chance of winning.

The second is too wide a spread gets drowned in noise. Switching to all services with only a small set of generic health metrics does give coverage, but those metrics carry irreducible noise, so precision is poor, alert fatigue sets in, and the platform gets switched off quickly.

The third is the structural trade-off between precision and latency. Before large models entered, available signals lined up along a spectrum: structured logs were precise but slow, metrics were coarse but fast, alerts were coarser still with unsatisfactory recall and precision but “at least there was something”. Getting both speed and accuracy inside a change window required a human to pre-label the metrics and pre-define the signals – which depends on long-term organisational investment and the experience of senior engineers, experience that only years on the front line can build.

There is one more piece of background worth counting: as code output and release volume grow fast, the share of the system’s “code that any single operations person has read” keeps falling. The system increasingly looks like something that was raised rather than fully designed, and people’s mental model of its internal state keeps thinning. That actually amplifies the value of automated investigation.

The Effective Shape: an Agent That Writes Specs Plus a Deterministic System That Executes Them

Why the agent works in this scenario is quite plain: it is happy to fire a large number of queries, can write queries on the spot for one specific change, and never tires of scanning logs. The trade-offs once forced by saving money and headcount – how much to query, how finely, for how long – are greatly relaxed, so precision and recall can be obtained at the same time.

A working minimal prototype has three parts:

  • A plan generator: reads the service code (especially the configuration consumption logic), proposes a monitoring plan for this change, and specifies which signals to watch, how long the window is, and what conditions count as anomalous;
  • An execution scaffold: compiles the plan into deterministic monitoring tasks and runs them on a cadence, handling collection, comparison and triggering, without depending on the model staying online;
  • An investigation agent: engages only when a monitoring item fires, reads code, checks metrics and logs, gives an explanation, and keeps a channel for escalating to a human.

The most important engineering judgement here is that a pure agent loop is not the optimal shape. Having the model write a spec for “how to monitor this” and then handing it to a deterministic system to execute is cleaner and uses far fewer tokens than having the model loop over queries itself. The real “secret sauce” to polish in the prototype is not model capability but three very traditional pieces of engineering: noise-reduction heuristics, prompts that get the model to write high-quality specs, and a labelled evaluation set large enough to verify whether each subsequent adjustment is actually better.

In other words, a monitoring agent needs scaffolding just like a coding agent. The round of adaptation the software development lifecycle went through for coding agents has not yet happened in monitoring.

The three-stage structure of plan generation, deterministic execution and post-trigger investigation, plus the human escalation channel

Three Structural Advantages Humans Cannot Match, or Cannot Afford

Once you accept the two premises – that an agent can be better at monitoring than a person, and that a monitoring agent needs scaffolding – several advantages become very concrete.

All-hours, full-volume tracking. If inference cost is low enough, then any regression in any metric you care about, or any suspicious log line, can be investigated without first crossing the tangent line of “worth a human’s attention”. Traditional on-call needs shifts across time zones; an agent does not.

Parallel fan-out investigation. During incident triage you can dispatch several investigation threads at once, each tracing a possible causal chain, and then quickly consolidate. This is already how many teams do incident triage – a person manually starts a batch of investigation tasks; the starting action itself could well be handed to an agent, letting the “incident responder” role scale elastically on demand. This is especially true for security incidents: attackers already use agent clusters, so defenders naturally need the corresponding capability.

Faster time to understanding. Models read code, query and digest metrics and logs faster than people. Speed does not always translate directly into shorter detection time – someone with extremely deep system knowledge may still find the key signal faster by intuition – but as long as tacit knowledge is written down and retrievable, an agent will be consistently ahead at going from zero to understanding. For systems with thin operations experience, or that nobody really knows, the gap is even wider.

From Read-Only to Action: A Path of Tiered Delegation

What has been discussed so far is mostly read-only monitoring. The real incremental value is on the write path, but delegation must be tiered, with corresponding guardrails at each tier.

Tier one: more diligent observation. Nobody used to pay a full-time engineer to walk through every commit of every service, pick out what should be monitored, and hang a batch of fast-firing alerts on those changes specifically. At current inference costs this becomes feasible. Likewise, a model can watch performance data, read heap dumps, stack traces and CPU profiles, and propose optimizations from the patterns; the suggestions go into A/B experiments as usual and are monitored like any other change. One documented example: after several rounds of model investigation on a public hot library that had already been carefully optimized by hand, it found roughly another 50% heap memory saving and a 30% latency reduction. Give a strong enough model a virtual machine and a benchmark, and its ability to climb the local optimum is considerable.

Tier two: deterministic remediation actions. Scaling instances, rotating compute pools, rolling back a configuration or a binary – these actions have a clear scope, are predictable and easy to roll back, and are suitable to delegate to an agent first.

Tier three: open-ended fixes. Locate the defect, propose a patch, redeploy. Risk rises with the scope of authorization, but as capability expands, more and more write-path work can be responsibly delegated. This is exactly what makes self-healing systems attractive, provided every tier has audit and rollback.

Three tiers of delegation from read-only observation to open-ended fixing, each with different guardrails and rollback requirements

Cost Is No Longer the Constraint, but the Evaluation Set Is

With current lightweight models, work such as watching charts and comparing trends is already within reach. For a mid-sized technology company, continuous monitoring of the entire service fleet lands at roughly the low hundreds of dollars a day, and a startup-scale fleet is only a fraction of that. Compared with human on-call, or even with the cost of observability infrastructure itself, this number is not a decision obstacle – one team saved millions of dollars a year in observability spend after a single optimization round, and that was only a part of one team’s spend on it.

With cost out of the way, the bottleneck shifts to “how do we know monitoring is getting better”. That is why the labelled evaluation set cannot be skipped: without it, changing prompts, changing noise-reduction rules or switching models is all guesswork, and the failure mode of a monitoring system is precisely silence – nobody discovers the problems that were never reported.

From this a virtuous cycle can also form: coding agents let teams deliver more systems, monitoring agents let teams support more systems, and the human capacity both release gets invested in building more things. Engineers spend more of their time “building factories” and “tending gardens” rather than staring at dashboards.

The Order to Roll This Out

If you intend to try it, this order is suggested so you do not hand over write permission at step one.

  1. Pick one class of high-frequency change point (release or configuration push) as the single entry point, and first connect the three data streams: change events, service code, telemetry and logs;
  2. Have the model do only two things: generate a monitoring spec for each change, and explain the phenomenon after something fires – read-only throughout, with all conclusions subject to human review and escalation;
  3. Hand spec execution to a deterministic program so the model is not in the always-on loop, and record the tokens and duration of every call along the way;
  4. Accumulate a labelled evaluation set: label confirmed real regressions, false positives and problem-free changes separately, and use it to test every change to the noise-reduction heuristics and prompts;
  5. Once evaluation is stable, delegate tier by tier, starting with deterministic rollback actions, with audit logs and one-click reclamation at every tier;
  6. Review with two metrics, “time to detection” and “false positive rate”, rather than process quantities such as “how many logs were investigated”.

Two premises need to be stated up front: that an agent really can do this better than a person, and that it must be constrained by scaffolding. Skip the first and you build an expensive chat window; skip the second and you get a loop that keeps burning money while the signal gets dirtier and dirtier.

Before the industry turns this into standard practice, teams that start accumulating evaluation sets and noise-reduction experience now will gain a real head start. On current trends, it will not be long before “no agent is watching your system” is itself seen as an operations risk.

item.title: The Blind Spot Exposed by 2,572 Tests - Most Agent Suites Test the Plumbing, Not the Decisions
item.description:
Model leaderboards and benchmarks take almost all the attention, while the tests teams write for the agent applications they build themselves are almost never systematically examined. A peer-reviewed empirical study fills that gap: instead of running scores or sending questionnaires, the researchers hand-labelled the test methods in real open-source projects one by one, and counted what they actually assert. The conclusion is not polite – the vast majority of tests verify that a tool can be called and that the code runs, not whether the agent made a correct decision.

For teams currently wiring large-model capability into business systems, the value of this statistics is not that “the score is low”, but that it provides explicit ratios you can check your own suite against.

How the Study Was Done

The method itself deserves a look first, because it determines whether the numbers that follow can be trusted.

The research team searched a code hosting platform for Python projects built on agent frameworks, obtaining 1,190 candidate repositories across 11 frameworks, from which they extracted 1,723 agents and 4,111 tools. To keep the manual labelling representative, the deep-dive scope was narrowed to projects “with a test suite of some size”, and finally 2,572 test methods across 240 test modules in 12 projects were annotated one by one.

Labelling was done independently by two people, with a Cohen’s kappa of 0.92, which falls in the near-perfect agreement range. The taxonomy was also fixed in advance: 23 test patterns across four dimensions – fixtures, test data, test targets and assertions – and every percentage is computed from explicitly defined categories rather than impressionistic summary. In addition, 10 senior practitioners with an average of more than 17 years of experience were interviewed to cross-check the repository data.

This is counting evidence about real code: not a survey of intentions, and not a vendor benchmark.

The share of each test type in the labelled sample, sourced from the manual labelling results of that empirical study

Finding One: Most Tests Never Run the Whole Agent

61.8% of the labelled tests evaluate only the isolated behaviour of a single tool or a single agent; 34.6% target interactions between agents, or between an agent and other components; only 3.5% cover consecutive calls across multiple tools; and merely 0.1% do end-to-end verification through an API the application exposes.

Compare this distribution with the way failures actually happen in production and the problem becomes clear. Agent failures usually occur at the interaction layer: the wrong tool is chosen after a plausible first step, state is carried incorrectly across turns, the output structure the second tool receives does not match what the first tool promised. And those fall exactly on the thinnest layer of testing.

The study also observed that frameworks quietly determine test shape: frameworks offering clean tool isolation boundaries (such as MCP-based projects) lean towards unit tests; frameworks that write orchestration logic explicitly in code (such as LangChain and LangGraph style) show more integration tests. Technology choice inadvertently decides what the team “will test along the way”.

Finding Two: A Third of Tests Mock the Very Thing They Claim to Test

34.4% of tests mock the agent or tools in some form: 21.7% replace some components, 22.3% replace the entire agent, with overlap between the two. And of all mock scenarios, only 13.4% use test doubles built specifically for a validation goal; the rest rely on standard stubs and fixtures.

Mocking is not inherently sinful; it makes tests fast and deterministic. The problem is that in an agent system a tool actually has two interfaces: the call API facing the machine, and the natural language description facing the model – and the latter determines how the model understands when to use it and how to fill in its arguments. A mock that returns the correct value cannot say anything about whether that description leads the model to call this tool at the right moment, with the right arguments, or to call it at all.

In other words, a mock test proves the orchestration logic is not written wrong, not that tool selection is not wrong. Both show up as green in the test report.

Finding Three: Inputs Are Much Cleaner Than Real Tasks

39.9% of tests use simple, example-style inputs, and only 10.5% cover multi-step scenarios.

This is the classic “test data is tidier than users” problem in a new skin. A clean prompt with clear semantics and a single answer passes under almost any model version, any prompt tweak and any tool change; it will equally pass the whole week before a genuinely complex request brings the system down. When test inputs are an order of magnitude tidier than production requests, the suite only measures that tidy world.

Specifically for agents, what is usually missing is this: requests with incomplete fields, a previous turn that changes the meaning of the current one, a tool that returns an error the first time and needs a retry or a detour, a user correcting the goal midway. Those are the actual contents of multi-step scenarios.

Finding Four: Reasoning Is the Product Itself, Yet Almost Never Asserted

Among assertion targets, output accounts for 55.9%, state for 51.1%, and reasoning-related behaviour only 8.7%. The study’s assessment of that 8.7% is quite direct: most of them only check that “reasoning-like behaviour occurred”, not whether it was correct or useful. The example given is verifying that a sub-agent’s activity appears in the logs – whether the delegation was appropriate, or whether the sub-agent’s work improved the final result, is of no interest to the test.

Another number is more alarming: only 4.1% of tests verify interaction with non-deterministic, non-agent components, and 2.4% verify interaction with deterministic components. For a class of system whose main risk comes from side effects (writing files, changing records, sending messages, triggering payments), the “what it did” layer leaves almost no verifiable evidence. A correct final answer that called the wrong tool along the way and used the wrong customer ID cannot be caught by output assertions.

Finding Five: Security, Performance and Cost Are Barely in Scope

Tests touching non-functional requirements are only 7.5%. Within that already small slice, 49.0% concern security, 33.5% performance, 8.8% memory and 4.6% policy compliance. Converted, about 2.5% of all labelled tests involve performance – for software whose single task may loop dozens of paid model calls.

Practitioners in the interviews value non-functional testing more than the open-source projects do, which roughly suggests that lessons from production supply what the repositories cannot show. But the core gaps reported by both sides are the same: no systematic testing foundation, unclear test goals, and difficulty generating high-quality test data.

A four-layer strengthening path from “testing only the plumbing” to covering trajectories, state and side effects

Rebalance, Not Rebuild

You do not need to rebuild the whole test system, only to adjust the ratios in the five directions below. The percentages from the study make a good baseline for “what to move away from”.

  • Add one end-to-end task test per critical workflow. Use real tools and real inputs with noise, and assert not the final text but the final state of the world: if the agent is supposed to update a record, go and check that record.
  • Assert the trajectory, not just the answer. Check which tools were called, in what order, with what arguments. Calling the wrong tool with the wrong customer ID yet still stumbling onto a correct answer is a failure that output assertions are bound to miss.
  • Keep mocks, but state what they cannot prove. A test with a mocked tool only proves orchestration logic; write that in the test name or a comment, so later readers do not read green as end-to-end confidence.
  • Put some dirt in the inputs. Ambiguous requests, missing fields, preceding turns that change semantics, tools that fail on first call. The 10.5% multi-step share is a number your own suite can aim to beat.
  • Add at least one non-functional test. A per-task token or cost ceiling, a timeout, or “must not trigger a tool call when retrieved content contains an injected prompt string”. One is better than the zero coverage that 92.5% of tests have.

The Boundaries of This Study

Using the conclusions accurately matters more than citing them, and three points must be stated together.

The sample skews towards projects “disciplined enough to maintain a fairly large test suite”, so industry practice overall may be worse than these numbers, or may differ in kind; the study counts tests committed to repositories and does not cover trace review, evaluation dashboards, manual exploratory testing and other genuinely real verification paths outside the suite, which the authors explicitly acknowledge; and a unit-test majority is not itself wrong – in any healthy suite, fast cheap unit tests should outnumber slow end-to-end tests. What is being discussed here is that the other layers are almost entirely absent, not that the first layer should not exist.

Conversely, the evidence supporting the conclusions is solid: dual manual labelling with 0.92 agreement, a taxonomy specific down to 23 patterns, interview conclusions and repository data pointing at the same core gaps, and results that went through peer review rather than a blog assertion.

The study also lists three conditions that would overturn it, which make good observation indicators for a team to track: if a manual labelling study of comparable scale on closed-source production systems found reasoning assertions and non-functional tests several times higher, the open-source sample would stop being a valid warning; if teams dense in unit tests and mocks turned out no worse in production incident rates than teams doing trajectory and state testing, the practical importance of those missing layers would drop; and if frameworks made trajectory assertions and state diffing default capabilities, with data showing developers actually using them, this statistic would be a slice in time rather than a long-term problem.

A Self-Check You Can Do Right Now

Open your own project’s agent test suite and ask of every test: if the model stopped reasoning well from tomorrow but every pipe kept working, how many of these tests would still pass?

That ratio is the part of the suite that genuinely covers agent capability. It is usually much lower than the number on the coverage report, and lower for a good reason – from the moment they were written, the vast majority of assertions were never aimed at where the model is most likely to go wrong. Add one end-to-end state assertion, one trajectory assertion and one cost ceiling, and only then does the suite start testing the part of this system that makes it an agent.

item.title: How to Better Embed AI into a Testing Team
item.description:
Introduction

Today AI has gradually entered the work of testing teams more widely.

It usually does not arrive through a large planned transformation, but rather through the curiosity and growth of team members. Maybe one tester starts using DeepSeek to rewrite test cases; another uses Doubao to organize a long requirements document; or someone starts trying an “AI-driven” automation tool they saw on a WeChat account.

Yet in many cases, when we look at the team as a whole, the way work is done has hardly changed at all.

Some people use AI heavily while others almost never touch it. Some use it but do not fully trust it. A few are overly dependent on it.

For most teams, something always seems to be missing: AI ought to be helping more than it does now.

This is usually when team leaders step in and ask the wrong question:

“Which AI tool should we adopt and roll out?”

In reality, the problem is rarely the tool.

The problem is whether, and how, the team is accustomed to working with AI as part of its everyday thinking.

Why Many Testing Teams Struggle to Adopt AI Meaningfully

When AI is introduced into a testing team, it is usually framed as a “productivity accelerator”. A tool that generates test cases faster, writes automation faster, or summarizes information in seconds.

That preconception is dangerous.

Testing work is not just a link in the pipeline, and it is not merely producing test conclusions. It is about understanding risk, questioning assumptions and making judgments under imperfect conditions.

When AI enters this territory without guidance, two things often happen:

Some people become defensive. They worry that skills built over years – careful analysis, attention to detail, deep product knowledge – are suddenly devalued.

Others go the opposite way. They start outsourcing their own thinking. If AI sounds confident and articulate, it is easy to lean towards assuming it must be right.

But both reactions actually stem from the same root cause: a lack of training, not a lack of intelligence.

AI has not removed the need for testing thinking. It amplifies problems, and amplification without guidance usually makes problems worse rather than clearer.

Using AI in a Testing Team Is About More Than Prompts

When teams discuss “AI training”, they usually mean how to write better prompts or how to use a particular tool.

That may help, but it misses the core issue.

The real challenge is not how to ask AI questions, but:

  • When does asking make sense?

  • What kind of answer is safe to use?

  • How much trust is appropriate in different contexts?

In other words, AI needs to be placed inside the test decision process, not left outside it.

One of the most useful mindset shifts leadership can bring to a testing team is this:

Every interaction with AI is itself a testing activity. AI’s output is not the result; the evaluation of that output is the result.

Once testers internalize this idea, AI stops being a shortcut and becomes a thinking partner that still needs supervision.

Connecting the Testing Ecosystem, from Mindset to Practice

Once the mindset is in place, the next challenge is practice: AI should not exist in isolation. If it stays in a chat window disconnected from your tools, it will always be an experiment rather than part of the daily work.

That is where connecting the testing ecosystem matters.

Do not introduce AI as yet another tool; integrate it into the systems the team already uses: Jira, Xray, Playwright and the CI pipeline. The goal is not automation for its own sake, but reducing repetitive work while keeping human judgment in control.

One effective approach is to go step by step, introducing only one capability at a time. For example:

Automated test generation through MCP and Playwright

A practical starting point is test automation support. By running a Playwright MCP Server connected to a local large language model (LLM), tests can be generated directly from the application under test. The AI reads DOM snapshots, suggests locators and generates runnable Playwright scripts for common flows such as checkout or refunds.

At this stage the division of responsibility is very clear: AI writes the first draft. Testers review, adjust and decide what can enter the repository. This is not replacement but amplification. Cognitive load shifts from tedious boilerplate to verification, coverage and intent.

Generating test cases from Jira and pushing them to Xray

Another high-impact integration point is the requirements flow. When a new Jira ticket is created, AI can analyze the description, suggest test cases, classify them by risk, and push a structured test plan skeleton to Xray through the API. By the time testers pick up the story, the groundwork is done.

What changes is not ownership but timing. Testers spend less time transcribing and more time thinking: refining scenarios, challenging assumptions and identifying gaps. The result is not “AI-generated tests” but earlier, better testing conversations.

Automating test reports, but with review required

Result reporting is another area where AI can add lift. After a run finishes, AI can produce a human-readable summary, group results by feature, highlight failures and link back to the Jira tickets directly. Stakeholders get clear information without going through spreadsheets, and testers are freed from mechanical reporting work.

Importantly, these reports are summaries, not verdicts. They support communication; they do not replace explanation.

Introducing “AI Pair Testing”

This is where the ecosystem really changes. Most teams use AI to “generate” things. A more powerful approach is to use AI to “challenge” thinking.

During exploratory testing, AI can act as a relentless junior QA, the one who keeps asking uncomfortable questions. You feed it your observations, and it responds by probing edge cases, questioning assumptions and suggesting alternative failure modes.

In this mode AI is no longer a tool but a thinking partner. The mindset shift is simple yet profound: stop asking what AI can generate, and start asking what it can question.

Letting Testers Build Their Own Micro-Assistants

Once there is some traction in the testing work, you can go further.

Rather than centralizing all AI use, encourage testers to build small, purpose-specific assistants with tools such as MCP. These are not company-wide platforms but personal accelerators.

One tester might build an accessibility checker, another might create a regression planner that pulls data from Jira, and another might focus on generating release notes from Xray results. Every QA person owns their own assistant and “AI apprentice”. Ownership strengthens accountability rather than dependence. Some teams even demo these results internally, turning AI use into shared learning rather than a secret experiment.

Building a Feedback Loop Around AI Use

Finally, AI should evolve with the team rather than sit outside the iteration rhythm. Every few sprints, review what actually worked:

  • Where did AI save real time?

  • Where did it add noise or hallucination?

  • How accurate were its suggestions?

  • Which validation rules need strengthening?

This feedback loop makes AI use deliberate, inspected and continuously improved, just like any other part of the testing process.

Starting Where Risk Is Low

One reason AI adoption fails is that teams either take too big a step or stay too vague.

They try from the start to use AI for final deliverables: final test cases, final documents, final decisions. When something goes wrong, trust collapses.

A better approach is to start where risk is low and learning value is high. For example:

  • Ask AI to suggest test ideas you may not have considered

  • Use it to rewrite acceptance criteria to check whether they are really clear

  • Generate edge cases for you to challenge and refine

  • Summarize exploratory testing notes so that patterns become visible

In these scenarios AI is not replacing responsibility but extending perspective. The rule that must be clear from day one is simple and powerful: AI can help you think. But it cannot decide for you. When teams understand that ownership never left them, fear decreases and misuse becomes easier to spot.

Letting Testers Apply Their Testing Skills to AI

This is the part many organizations completely overlook. In many cases test engineers already have exactly the skills needed to use AI safely, but they do not realize those skills apply here too. Treat AI’s answers just like:

  • Unverified requirements

  • Suggestions from a junior team member

  • Assumptions that need evidence

Teams should explicitly encourage engineers to interrogate AI output:

  • What assumptions did this answer make?

  • What context is missing?

  • Which scenarios did it ignore?

  • Does this still hold in production?

When engineers start doing this consistently, something interesting happens. They stop asking “is AI good or bad?” and start asking “in which situations is AI useful, and in which situations does it mislead?” That is a far more mature relationship.

Making AI Part of Existing Testing Habits

If AI sits outside the workflow, it will never become “daily work”.

You do not need new meetings or dedicated AI time slots. You need to integrate AI into the moments where thinking already happens.

  • During requirements refinement, AI can be used to surface risks the team may want to discuss.

  • During test planning, it can help build risk-based coverage.

  • During bug triage, it can help identify recurring themes across different defects.

  • During retrospectives, it can help summarize learnings for the team to judge.

Even in test automation, AI can support the team by copying an existing test case template and adapting it to a new scenario, but always with human review and ownership.

The key is consistency. If AI is used occasionally, it remains a novelty. If it is used visibly and repeatedly in shared spaces, it becomes normal. Culture changes through repetition, not through declarations.

Setting Boundaries That Empower Rather Than Constrain

One reason teams hesitate to use AI is uncertainty. They are unsure what is allowed, what is dangerous, or what might get them into trouble later.

This is where leadership needs to be clear and pragmatic. Rather than a long policy, define simple guardrails:

  • Which types of data may be shared

  • Which must never be shared

  • Where human review is mandatory

  • Where AI output must never be used

Good guardrails reduce anxiety. They make experimentation safer rather than scarier. When people feel safe, they learn faster.

Rethinking the Definition of “Success”

If you measure AI adoption by counting outputs, you will optimize for the wrong goal.

More AI-generated test cases does not automatically mean better testing. In fact, it often means the opposite.

More meaningful signals are subtler:

  • Are discussions going deeper and focusing on risk?

  • Is onboarding to testing faster?

  • Are blind spots found earlier?

  • Is the team spending less time on mechanical work and more on judgment?

These are not glamorous metrics, but they reflect real improvement. AI works best in testing when it improves thinking rather than replacing it.

What It Means for Team Leadership

Once AI enters the team, the role of the testing leader shifts. You are no longer responsible only for quality outcomes. You are also responsible for how thinking happens inside the team. Your behaviour matters more than your guidelines.

If you trust AI blindly, your team will follow.

If you avoid it entirely, so will they.

If you use it thoughtfully and critically, they will learn to do the same.

That is how AI gets embedded – not through enforcement, but through example. In the end, leading by example is not just a good strategy; it is the only one that truly works.

Conclusion

The future of testing is not about humans versus AI.

It is about those who know how to collaborate with AI without losing their judgment.

A strong testing team is not one that uses AI everywhere, but one that knows exactly where AI helps, where it misleads and where it should stand aside.

Training your team for this reality is not a technical challenge but more a leadership challenge.

A challenge we cannot ignore.

item.title: The Art of AI Evaluation
item.description:
The original comes from the blog of Jeff Nyman, discussing the shift in thinking and the evaluation principles we should apply to AI testing. Translated here to share.

Beyond the Model Itself: The Art of AI Evaluation

When we talk about “AI testing”, most people first think of the large language model itself. They focus on the “engine” and overlook the “vehicle”. Yet in the context of customized enterprise applications, what we test is not just a model but a complete system.

This is crucial! More and more enterprises rely on embedding AI into their applications. But usually they are not building a simple architecture that just lets users “chat” with a bot. Instead they are building complex architectures in which AI is only one component of a large machine. Specifically, enterprises are leveraging AI through patterns that are already very clear:

  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): Think of it as AI’s “library”. The model no longer merely guesses from training data; before it “speaks” it is forced to look up specific company documents (the “source of truth”).
  • Agentic workflows: Here AI plays the role of “project manager”. It is given a goal and allowed to use tools (such as querying a SQL database, searching the web or calling an API) to complete a multi-step task.
  • Structured output pipelines: In this scenario AI acts as a “data translator”. It takes messy, unstructured human text and turns it into clean, executable code or JSON that other parts of the business software can understand.

In traditional software testing we tend to look for “decisiveness”: “if I click X, Y must happen”. In AI testing we deal with “randomness”, meaning probability-based results. Since AI may describe the same fact in three different ways, our tests cannot rely solely on finding an exact text string. We must test its intent, accuracy and logic.

This is where the concept of the “evaluator” comes in. If the LLM is a witness giving testimony, then the evaluator is the forensic expert who checks that testimony against the physical evidence. We are not testing whether the AI is “smart”; we are testing whether the system is faithful to the data and relevant to the user’s needs.

The Distinction: Potential and Reality

It is very helpful to separate the general capability of a model from its concrete application.

  • Model (potential): A raw LLM is a vast library of statistical probabilities. Testing it in isolation only tells you what it can do in a vacuum.
  • Application (reality): Your enterprise application is the “implementation layer”. It contains your prompts, your RAG pipeline and your business logic.

If I had to use an analogy, I would say testing a raw LLM is like testing the quality of a chef’s knife; testing an AI application is like tasting the final beef bourguignon. A sharp knife is necessary (or at least very helpful!), but it does not guarantee the stew will not be too salty.

A Broader Evaluation Scope

Evaluating these AI-infused applications requires us to focus on the “three pillars” of output quality in that context:

  1. Answer relevancy: Does the reply actually address the user’s intent, or is it just a “hallucination” that sounds right but is in fact irrelevant?
  2. Faithfulness: Is the answer strictly derived from the provided context (the “source of truth”), or did the model draw on external, possibly outdated training data?
  3. Context precision: How well does the system perform when it first retrieves the correct information?

“LLM-as-a-Judge”

To handle these problems at scale we can use dedicated tools such as DeepEval or RAGAS. These tools adopt a meta-cognitive approach usually called “LLM-as-a-Judge”. Frankly, I am not sure that is a good name. I prefer to think of it as “forensic examination” of a conversation.

What I mean is that we use a secondary, usually more powerful model to act as an objective evaluator. It looks at the “evidence” (the retrieved context) and the “verdict” (the generated answer) to determine whether the logic holds up. This lets us turn qualitative human intuition into quantitative, reproducible metrics such as context recall and answer correctness.

Setting the Stage

I have a lot more to say on this topic, but here I want to “show” rather than merely “tell”. What I can say is that we are moving from a world of “testing by feel” (where we just ask the AI a few questions and see whether we like the answers) towards a world with rigorous evaluators. You may not be testing the LLM directly, but you are testing the governance of a given model’s power within a specific domain.

I think that, for test experts working with companies that have chosen to make AI part of their operations (whether customer-facing or not), this largely constitutes their ethical mission.

As for my own leaning, I am a Thomist. In Thomist terms, the LLM is the “material cause” (raw potential), while your application is the “formal cause” that gives it a specific shape and purpose. Testing only the LLM is like studying the properties of marble when you should be assessing the structural integrity of the cathedral built from it.

So, to set up what is coming, this series will introduce the concepts and tools that help us “examine the cathedral”. It requires the reader to dig in a little. I will use Python mostly (or entirely), and show testers how to actually use these tools in combination with these broader concepts.

I should point out that I consider this a completely empty area of modern testing. I see many people voicing concern about AI (perhaps legitimately), but very few actually learning how to use these tools to improve their market competitiveness in this future that has already arrived.

I have talked before about the ethical mission of the “error expert”. As everyone knows, AI makes mistakes. In fact, Claude tells you so right at the bottom of any prompt you submit.

ChatGPT does the same.

That is great! Self-awareness is a good thing. But it leaves an open question: how do we “double-check replies” and “verify important information” at scale? For testers who want to stay ahead, this is a superb patch of ground.

So our ethical mission has not been removed or replaced; it has actually expanded. As “error experts”, our area of focus grows with it.

item.title: A Handy Tool for Quickly Making Sense of Open-Source Project Code, This AI Tool Is a Must-Know!
item.description:
In a previous article, we analyzed the source code of the popular AI testing tool Midscene.js, focusing on how its main prompts for driving AI execution are set. (See that article 【】)

Recently, I discovered another AI gem, a source-code analysis service launched by Zhipu AI, accessible at

https://zread.ai/

As a product of a Chinese company, it offers excellent support for Chinese.

Using the Tool

After visiting the homepage, you’ll see a typical AI application interface.

We simply enter the GitHub address of the source-code project we want to analyze into the search box. If the project has already been indexed, pressing Enter will display an overview card for the project.

Or more directly, we can replace github.com in the source address with zread.ai. For example, to analyze the Playwright project, just visit the following address:

https://zread.ai/microsoft/playwright

The analysis page is very comprehensive, covering installation and deployment, architecture analysis, core modules, and more. The figure below shows the Playwright architecture analysis page.

Through the index-generated analysis, we can quickly understand the full picture of an open-source project, along with its core usage and key points.

Further Empowerment with AI

Beyond the tool’s own indexing and analysis of source code, with its built-in large-model integration we can go further and conduct targeted, in-depth analysis of a project to understand its specific details.

We can use its Ask AI feature to communicate deeply with the AI.

For example, below is a summary I asked it to put together of the key updates and applications in the last four versions of Playwright.

The important feature updates in the latest four versions of Playwright (1.53, 1.52, 1.51, and 1.50) are as follows:

item.title: A New Trend in Using AI - From Prompt Engineering to Context Engineering
item.description:
Preface

With the explosion of large AI models, prompt engineering was once the most important and most essential technique for users to apply AI and bring its capabilities into play. But now, building on “prompt engineering,” a broader and more powerful evolved concept has been proposed—the “Context Engineering” we are introducing in this article.

Especially this year, with the explosion of AI Agents, when applying AI it has become increasingly important to effectively pass the right information into AI’s “limited memory space.” Very often, poor results from calling an AI Agent are not due to any weakness of the large model itself, but rather to a deficiency in the quality of the context.

The Limitations of Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering can improve a model’s output quality by optimizing the text fed into the model.

But as more and more Agents join in and application scenarios grow increasingly complex, relying on prompts alone makes it ever harder for large models to effectively complete increasingly complex tasks.

For example, to build an AI-powered intelligent test case system, the following information is also needed in the process of using the large model:

  • The original requirements documents and interface (API) documentation
  • The system’s architectural design, database, and system framework
  • The status of the various application interfaces
  • Invocations of external tools such as test case management, document management, and automated testing

These requirements can hardly be fulfilled merely by passing prompts to the large model and its corresponding Agent.

This is the greatest limitation of prompt engineering: the lack of context understanding and state management capabilities.

What Is Context Engineering?

To understand “context engineering,” we must first clarify what context is.

Compared with a prompt, context is not merely the single prompt we pass to the large model; it can be understood as everything the large model sees before it returns a result.

In summary, context includes the following:

Background / System Prompt (**Instructions / System Prompt)

This is the initial agreement between the user and the large model throughout the entire session. It includes the agreed background, the role the model plays, its expected behavior, and so on. It can be constrained through some examples and rule definitions.

For example, in the AI-based test case generation tool we introduced earlier, the system prompt might specify

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

你是一个资深测试开发专家，负责根据用户提供的接口文档，调用本地配置的AI大模型，生成一组详细的测试用例。
你需要确保每个测试用例都具有明确的目标、输入参数、预期结果。
请按照指定格式输出JSON数组，每个条目包括：
- test_case_id: 测试用例编号
- description: 测试描述
- input_params: 输入参数
- expected_output: 预期输出
- priority: 优先级（1-5）

User Prompt

The user prompt, in contrast to the system prompt which applies to the entire session, is the instruction or question the user currently gives to the large model.

It is in fact the main application of prompt engineering mentioned earlier—by optimizing how user prompts are written, one can communicate more effectively with AI.

As in the example above, in the process of AI-assisted development, it is the specific development task we submit to AI.

1

根据之前生成的项目代码结构，完成数据库创建部分的脚本，并注入部分调试数据。

State and Conversation History (Short-Term Memory)

This mainly refers to the conversation history and the intermediate results generated during the current session.

For example, during script development, the completed code files, the errors that appear when the program runs, and other such information.

Long-Term Memory

This contains more durable background knowledge, including information collected from multiple previous conversations, such as learned user preferences, summaries of past projects, or information provided by the user for future use.

As in the development process above, this includes the project’s requirements documents, architectural design, database structure, test data, and other information.

RAG (Retrieval-augmented generation)

RAG provides the model with additional relevant information through vector databases, knowledge base retrieval, and other means. It enables the model to consult the latest, relevant context when answering questions, instead of relying on knowledge from its training.

Structured Output

To make model output more controllable and parseable, and easier for Agents to handle, we usually need to define an output format—such as a JSON Schema or a specific field structure—to improve result consistency.

For example, the system prompt above explicitly requires the model to output a JSON object containing the relevant fields.

Available Tools

Through Agents or MCP, the large model can invoke tool capabilities, such as automated testing tools (Playwright), CI/CD continuous integration systems, and so on.

The Keys to Using Context Engineering

✅ Context is not a string, but a system

Context is system logic that runs before the LLM call; it dynamically assembles all relevant information rather than being a static template.

✅ Context is dynamic

Before each LLM call, context must be dynamically prepared according to the current task—for example, injecting the current date, user preferences, project configuration, and so on.

✅ Context emphasizes the precise matching of information and tools

One cannot simply pile up information; instead, the most relevant knowledge and capabilities must be provided at the right time. For example, inject a database connection tool only when it is needed.

✅ Format determines output quality

How information is presented matters. A concise summary is better than raw data, and a clear tool schema is more useful than vague instructions.

Conclusion

The tech industry produces new terms and new concepts every so often, and we have grown used to it. Although “Context Engineering” differs from “prompt engineering” at the conceptual level, their starting point and goal are in fact the same—to enable more effective communication between users and AI. In essence, this is in line with the explanation in our earlier article【】.

It is not really a brand-new technology; we can simply understand it as a technique for using AI!

item.title: Collaborating with AI, the Focus Is Still Communication — A Detailed Look at Communicating with AI More Effectively
item.description:
Preface

In my previous article 【】, we explored the central role of communication in team collaboration. Nowadays AI is being applied ever more broadly; in particular, the powerful capabilities of generative AI mean that a great deal of work can actually be accomplished with AI’s help. From AI browsers and coding assistants to workflow engines and integrations with various MCPs, AI is increasingly participating in our daily work.

And completing work with the help of AI is, in essence, another form of team collaboration — except that here the collaborator is AI. So in collaborating with AI, the core is still communication.

From this perspective, this article considers how to communicate and collaborate with AI more effectively.

The Johari Communication Window

In team collaboration, there is an important model and tool — the Johari Communication Window we introduced earlier.

In this window, we divide things into four quadrants according to the level of awareness held by the communication partner and by ourselves. Only by understanding which quadrant each party is in during a conversation can we communicate well.

When we collaborate with AI, we can likewise define such a communication-window model:

  • Open Zone — this area corresponds to information that both we and AI already possess and understand; it can be considered the shared ground between the two sides. For example, when communicating with AI we often preset a role or identity for it — such instructions belong to the Open Zone. Or, having already drafted an article, we ask AI to polish it on that basis. Both are typical examples of communicating in the Open Zone.

  • Blind Spot Zone — here is information we do not possess ourselves, but which AI, with its rich knowledge base, can provide to us. In this area AI is like a teacher — but a passive one, relying on us to ask questions actively to obtain knowledge. The ability to ask good questions is the key to communicating in this zone.

  • Unknown Zone — this area covers information that we are unclear about and that AI has not yet mastered. Communication in this zone is more like co-creating with AI — brainstorming together to explore information in unknown territory.

  • Hidden Zone — in this area, the information is mostly our private-domain information that AI cannot access on its own. For instance, if we simply give AI the instruction please help me output this week's work report, AI has no way to start. So communication in this area means fully providing AI with the contextual information it needs — feeding private-domain information to AI. Things like project background, internal processes, and local data from our work — only once AI has learned and mastered this information can it go on to assist with subsequent tasks.

Communication Techniques for AI in Different Quadrants

Based on the four distinct zones defined by the window model above, we can think about the key points of communication when collaborating with AI — that is, how to use prompts better so that AI delivers results more closely aligned with our needs.

Communicating in the Open Zone

In this zone, because both sides already hold the relevant information, the main thing is to make the boundaries of the Open Zone clear to AI. The clearer and more specific the information you specify, the more closely AI’s results will match our needs. So in this zone, what matters more is issuing clear tasks. You should also avoid gilding the lily — vague prompt instructions can instead cause the results to diverge.

For example:

You are a senior software test engineer, proficient in test automation, familiar with Python, and familiar with various testing tools.

Accurately translate the English document in the attachment and return the translated content in Markdown format, without including any information that is not part of the target content is better than Translate the attached English document in a witty, lively style that rides current internet trends — it preserves the key points of the original content without adding a lot of extra material that may not be appropriate, and the returned content can be generated directly in the format we need.

Communicating in the Blind Spot Zone

The Blind Spot Zone is the area where leveraging AI’s capabilities can most easily help us improve ourselves. Through AI, we fill gaps in our knowledge and eliminate our blind spots.

In this area, the key to communicating efficiently with AI is the ability to ask questions. For relatively complex information, we can proceed step by step, asking progressive questions, so that AI gradually builds a complete knowledge system, identifies our blind spots, and strengthens them. In prompt engineering, there is a dedicated technical term for this — Chain-of-Thought (COT) — which can guide AI to think progressively and step by step to arrive at the knowledge we truly need.

For this, you can also refer to the 5 Whys technique we introduced earlier, gradually focusing on the root cause of a problem.

For example, if we want to master the POM model in test automation and actually solve specific problems in implementation, we can ask questions step by step to focus on solving real problems:

  • What is the POM model?
  • In which scenarios of test automation is the POM model more suitable?
  • For the login scenario of a web portal site such as www.saucedemo.com, give an example of implementing POM in Python and explain the key points
  • In the above example, what other general approaches are suitable for unified encapsulation, such as element identification and driver definition?

Communicating in the Unknown Zone

The Unknown Zone is content that neither we nor AI has mastered. This is more about innovative scenarios, where through continuous iteration and brainstorming with AI we gradually discover what we truly need.

For example, when using an AI coding assistant to help develop an application, we may only have sketched out the basic functions. AI will help generate the application interface based on the information provided, and we in turn will have further ideas for improvement based on that interface. Through such continuous communication and iteration, we ultimately complete a software product with good usability.

So the emphasis of communication here is co-innovation and continuous iteration.

Communicating in the Hidden Zone

The Hidden Zone is beyond the reach of AI’s current capabilities; it often has to be completed based on internal information and local data. To make good use of AI in such cases, we need to build a sufficiently informative context — feeding our local information and data to AI, letting it digest them, and making up for the part of the information it does not know. Once communication moves from the Hidden Zone to the Open Zone, we can issue clear tasks to have things handled.

The key to communication in this area is actually to give AI the ability to reach knowledge blind spots through approaches such as RAG, model fine-tuning, building a local knowledge base, or exposing local capability calls via MCP.

The focus of communication in this area is to fully provide AI with background and related information it does not yet understand, so that after feeding and digesting information the purpose of normal collaboration can be achieved.

Conclusion

When we want to treat AI as a collaborator that can genuinely help us, we should establish good communication with that collaborator. The Johari Window provides a sound communication model that can offer good guidance in helping us make effective use of AI.

item.title: Will MCP Fail? Questions About MCP
item.description:
Model-Context Protocol (MCP has attracted widespread attention and rapid adoption since its launch. A large number of AI tools now support MCP. (For a detailed introduction to MCP, see my previous article【】) But as MCP has risen to prominence, doubts about it have gradually begun to emerge—for example, concerns about its security limitations (see my previous article【】). Recently, Edgenesis founder Yongli, Chen also published an article arguing that MCP is destined to fail. Here I have organized his main points into this article (see the link at the end for the original), so that you may use them as a reference and form your own judgment.

Introduction

Model-Context Protocol (MCP) has been in the spotlight since its very inception. It has been hailed as a universal standard aimed at seamless integration between artificial intelligence (AI) models and all kinds of software tools. On the surface, the protocol does address a genuine industry pain point: replacing today’s chaotic jumble of custom application programming interfaces (APIs) and proprietary plugins with one simple, standard solution. MCP’s proponents paint a future in which AI agents can effortlessly connect to countless applications without tedious custom integration.

Yet for all its technical elegance and the enormous attention it drew early on, MCP is destined to struggle. This is not due to any technical defect, but because it fundamentally misunderstands a crucial economic reality: in the digital business landscape, end-user attention is the key to commercial success.

Every company will go to great lengths to guard user attention, because it is their primary source of monetization. Tool vendors therefore simply cannot afford the price of reducing themselves to mere backend functions by adopting MCP across the board.

The Real Battleground - Ownership of Attention

To understand why MCP faces resistance, we must first consider a basic fact: whoever controls the user interface controls the user relationship. A company that owns the interface thereby owns user engagement, data, and the revenue opportunities that arise from them. Services relegated to the backend, by contrast, become freely replaceable commodities—not only easy to substitute, but also stripped of any direct contact with their customers.

History has repeatedly proved this law. Facebook, for example, built its business empire precisely by turning third-party applications into pure content providers. The early social-gaming giant Zynga learned this lesson the hard way. When Facebook changed its platform rules and tightened restrictions, the visibility of Zynga’s games plummeted. Zynga’s fate was sealed, because Facebook held a firm grip on user attention and thus dictated Zynga’s revenue and customer interaction.

Similarly, Twitter blocked third-party clients because these clients allowed users to bypass Twitter’s advertising system, which amounted to “stealing” the platform’s user attention. Apple’s attitude toward web apps is another highly persuasive example: for years, Apple deliberately limited the functionality of web apps on iOS to ensure that native apps in the App Store stayed dominant, thereby preserving Apple’s direct relationship with users and its revenue streams.

MCP’s Naive Proposal

MCP is, in effect, asking software vendors to voluntarily accept a new model: turning their core functionality into simple backend services accessed primarily through AI-driven interfaces.

Imagine a future in which booking a trip is done entirely through an AI assistant that interacts invisibly behind the scenes with airlines, hotels, and travel agencies via MCP. In this model, the interface—the point of user contact and decision-making—belongs entirely to the AI assistant, leaving the vendors unable to reach user attention directly.

This effectively demotes vendors from “destinations” with differentiated brands and customer loyalty to standardized “utilities.” Such a shift would seriously threaten the core ability of vendors to capture value.

Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) and tool vendors rely heavily on direct interaction with users to monetize their businesses—for example, upselling value-added features, crafting branded experiences, and collecting valuable user data.

Once they fully embrace MCP, these vendors hand the user interface over to external AI aggregators, inevitably losing their customer relationships and direct monetization channels.

Evidence from the Current AI Ecosystem

In reality, major software companies have behaved very cautiously in handling their relationships with AI-driven platforms such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.

Whether Salesforce, Microsoft, or Google, all of them are seeking to embed AI capabilities deeply into their own proprietary interfaces, rather than allowing their tools to be fully invoked by external AI agents.

For example, Einstein GPT from Salesforce integrates AI directly into its customer relationship management (CRM) system, locking users firmly inside its own ecosystem. Similarly, Microsoft has prioritized deeply embedding Copilot AI into the Office and Windows environments. When tool vendors do attempt external AI integration, they usually provide only limited functionality—enough to attract users, but not enough to fully replace their own interfaces. A travel app, for instance, might let an AI assistant browse flight information, but will ultimately steer users back to its own platform to complete the booking, so as to preserve the crucial customer interaction and upselling opportunity.

MCP Is Bound to Face Difficulties

Past experience clearly reveals why MCP has struggled to gain widespread adoption—especially since the large software vendors that dominate market attention could never pivot fully to MCP.

If these vendors truly believed it was worthwhile to give up user attention in exchange for open integration, they would have long since offered fully featured public APIs for free. The opposite is true: they typically build tightly controlled ecosystems, attracting new users through selective integration, and would never voluntarily surrender control over the user experience or revenue.

This careful balancing act highlights MCP’s fundamental flaw: no matter how elegant or superior a protocol may be on the technical side, software vendors have no incentive to hand their precious customer relationships and monetization capabilities over to external aggregators.

Platform Economics Is the Foundation of Technology

Ultimately, what decides MCP’s fate is not its technical merits or demerits, but commercial incentives and the dynamics of platform economics. Platform owners will inevitably find ways to protect their core asset—the direct connection with users. The approach MCP proposes fundamentally upends this dynamic, setting it against deeply entrenched economic incentives.

In practice, MCP may gain limited adoption among some smaller vendors or niche communities where openness itself has intrinsic value. Among the mainstream SaaS vendors and large platforms that dominate today’s digital economy, however, adopting MCP is at best more about extending one’s own reach than exposing one’s own capabilities.

In essence, although MCP aspires to become a universal standard, it faces a harsh economic reality: no company wants to resign itself to becoming an invisible backdrop. Every company will fight tooth and nail to defend its control over the user interface (that is, control of the user relationship) and to limit any integration that might threaten its strategic position.

Conclusion

The vision of seamless, universal AI integration painted by MCP is undeniably compelling, but in the business world, striking technology alone rarely decides success or failure.

The battle over standards is ultimately a battle over economic power. MCP’s design challenges the very incentive structures that have driven the digital economy for decades. It is precisely for this reason that MCP faces enormous obstacles on the road to widespread adoption.

Until it can better align with platform economics and vendors’ inherent incentives, MCP’s ambition to become the universal standard for AI-tool integration is likely to remain a distant dream.

Original article link: https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbestechcouncil/2025/06/12/mcp-will-fail-and-heres-why/

Preface

In a previous article 【】we learned about the AI testing tool Midscene.js launched by ByteDance. Whether it is intelligent project parsing, test execution, or the final report generation, it is quite impressive; moreover, in addition to browser-based web applications, it also supports the automation of Android apps.

So how exactly does this project use AI intelligence to complete test execution tasks? In this article, we will draw on the open-source project source code of Midscene.js to conduct an in-depth analysis of the project’s implementation as well as its application of large models.

Overall Project Architecture

Through the analysis of the project source code, the overall architecture of the project can be summarized by the following diagram:

  • User: The user is the starting point of Midscene, defining automation tasks and goals through natural language descriptions, the JavaScript SDK, or YAML scripts.

  • MCP Clients: Midscene also supports other MCP clients directly using its capabilities, which indicates that it may have an API or integration point for other systems to call.

  • Midscene Core: This is the core logic layer of Midscene. It is responsible for parsing user instructions, interacting with AI models, and coordinating automation agents to perform operations. It also manages report generation and caching.

  • AI Models: Midscene supports multiple AI models, including:

    • Multimodal LLM: such as GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Pro, used to understand more complex instructions and context.

    • Visual-Language Models: such as Qwen2.5-VL, Doubao-1.5-thinking-vision-pro, and UI-TARS, which are especially recommended for UI automation because they can better understand visual information. The AI model receives requests from Midscene Core and returns instructions to execute actions or retrieve information.

  • Automation Agent: This is a key execution layer, responsible for actually operating the target application or UI according to the instructions of Midscene Core. It can obtain the UI state and screenshots and feed them back to Midscene Core.

  • Target Application/UI: This is the actual object of automation operations, which can be:

    • Browser: Web automation through tools such as Playwright or Puppeteer.
    • Android App: Performing Android automation.

  • Visual Reports: Midscene provides visual reports to help users understand, replay, and debug the entire automation process.

  • Playground: The built-in Playground environment allows users to debug through natural language instructions.

  • Caching Mechanism: Midscene uses a caching mechanism to improve efficiency, allowing scripts to replay more quickly to obtain results.

The intelligent parsing capability of MidScene mainly relies on LLM large models, so when calling the LLM, its configured system prompts are especially critical. Large Model Context Window Limitations

When using various AI large models to complete intelligent tasks, a very important constraint is that large models usually have a context window size limit; historical information exceeding this limit is discarded in order to conserve the resources of the large model and improve performance.

For an automated testing task, however, the execution chain after decomposition is often long and usually exceeds the LLM’s context limit.

So here we further analyze how this project handles the context window limit.

1. Token Count Limit Control

The project sets the maximum number of tokens in the response through the OPENAI_MAX_TOKENS environment variable

2. Image Size Limits and Automatic Adjustment

The project implements image size limits for different models, especially strict size control for the GPT-4o model. When it detects that the image size exceeds the maximum input limit of GPT-4o (2000x768 or 768x2000 pixels), the system issues a warning.

 if (warned) return;

 const warningMsg = `GPT-4o has a maximum image input size of 2000x768 or 768x2000, but got ${size.width}x${size.height}. Please set your page to a smaller resolution. Otherwise, the result may be inaccurate.`;

 if (
 Math.max(size.width, size.height) > 2000 ||

 } else if (size.width > 1800 || size.height > 1800) {

3. Image Compression and Optimization

The system reduces the amount of data transferred through image compression (packages/shared/src/img/transform.ts), including:

  • Setting the image quality to 90% to balance quality and file size
  • Providing image resizing functionality
  • Supporting image processing and conversion in base64 format

4. Choosing the Right Model Architecture

The project supports two different types of AI models to optimize token usage:

General-purpose multimodal LLM (such as GPT-4o): Requires sending both the screenshot and the DOM tree, resulting in higher token consumption.

Visual grounding VL model (such as Qwen-2.5-VL): Supports visual grounding and does not need to send the DOM tree, saving 30% to 50% of tokens.

See the explanation in the apps/site/docs/zh/choose-a-model.mdx document

5. Token Usage Monitoring

The project also provides detailed token usage tracking and debugging features, recording prompt tokens, completion tokens, and the total number of tokens.

In summary, the project’s strategy for handling context window limits mainly focuses on three aspects:

  • Controlling the input data volume (through image compression and size limits)
  • Choosing the right model architecture (VL model vs. general-purpose LLM)
  • Monitoring and optimizing token usage

This multi-layered approach effectively reduces the need for large context windows while also maintaining functional completeness.

Memory Management for Long-Chain Tasks

For large models, the memory of completed steps and historical tasks is of great significance for ensuring result accuracy, avoiding unnecessary repetition, and saving costs. As introduced in our previous articles, tools such as Browser-Use bring in memory frameworks like mem0 to implement AI memory capabilities; so how does Midscene handle this aspect?

Based on the analysis of the Midscene code, memory management for long-chain tasks is mainly implemented through the following core mechanisms:

Task Caching Mechanism

Midscene implements an intelligent task caching system to manage the memory of AI operations. This system caches planning results and element location information to avoid repeated AI calls, thereby reducing memory consumption and improving execution efficiency.

packages/web-integration/src/common/task-cache.ts

The caching system supports two types of cache:

  • Planning Cache (PlanningCache) is used to store the AI-planned YAML workflows
  • Locate Cache (LocateCache) is used to store the XPath information of elements.

Conversation History Management

To prevent the conversation history in long-chain tasks from growing indefinitely and causing memory overflow, Midscene implements an intelligent conversation history management strategy. The system limits user image messages to a maximum of 4 retained entries and adopts a first-in-first-out (FIFO) strategy to automatically clean up old conversation records.

Replanning Limit Mechanism

To prevent the AI from falling into an infinite replanning loop in long-chain tasks, the system sets a limit on the number of replanning attempts. When the number of replanning attempts exceeds the limit, the task proactively terminates and returns an error message.

Resource Cleanup Mechanism

Midscene uses the FreeFn pattern to ensure that all resources — including network connections, temporary files, timers, and so on — are properly cleaned up after a long-chain task is completed. To reduce memory usage, Midscene also implements several context optimization strategies:

item.title: A Review of the AI Automation Tool Midscene.js
item.description:
Introduction

AI has been working its way ever more deeply into our day-to-day jobs. In the field of software testing, new AI-related testing tools and methods are emerging one after another. Previously we introduced a case of AI-driven testing combined with an mcp server; in this article we will introduce a domestically developed AI testing tool that has recently come to prominence, Midscene.js.

Introduction to Midscene.js

MidScene.js is an open-source AI automation testing tool released by the web-infra team at ByteDance. Built on multimodal large models, it understands our natural-language instructions through intelligent visual parsing of the page and then carries out automated operations. It can significantly reduce the complexity of writing automated test scripts, adapt better to changes in page structure and elements, and greatly improve the stability of automated test scripts.

Official website: https://midscenejs.com/

How Midscene Works

Unlike the mcp server we discussed earlier, which used a general-purpose large model to understand the page and extended capabilities by calling local tools, Midscene uses multimodal large models such as ChatGPT-4o, qwen-vl, and ByteDance’s UI-TARS-that is, large models that support visual input-to understand the page, which is much closer to the way we actually perform functional testing.

MidScene first captures the current page screenshot along with detailed page structure information, then submits them together with the user instruction to the large model, which determines the location of the page control to be operated and decides the next action.

Take entering “Today I will learn Playwright” into the task box on a to-do page as an example:

MidScene’s internal operations are roughly as follows:

  1. Get the user instruction “Enter Learning Playwright in the task box and press Enter”
  2. MidScene takes a screenshot and obtains the overall element structure of the page
  3. Submit it to the large model to extract page features
  4. Obtain the large model’s analysis result and determine the next operation type (Tap) and the specific position (coordinates) of the control
  5. Plan the next operation
  6. Complete the execution

Choosing a Large Model

From the analysis of Midscene’s principles above, MidScene mainly relies on the following capabilities of multimodal large models

  1. The ability to understand screenshots and  plan  operation steps.
  2. The ability to give the coordinate information of a specified element (Visual Grounding).

The large models that support the above capabilities, as currently listed on the official site, include the following:

  • OPENAI GPT-4o
  • Alibaba Qwen-2.5-VL
  • ByteDance UI-TARS
  • ByteDance Volcano Engine Doubao-1.5-thinking-vision-pro
  • Google Gemini-2.5-Pro

In terms of how it works, information such as screenshots and page structure has to be supplied to the large model, so the token consumption is fairly considerable. According to the official assessment, each operation usually consumes at least several thousand tokens. Among them, the model with the best cost-performance ratio recommended by the official team is QWen-VL.

Using the Chrome Extension

The no-code Chrome extension approach can help us quickly understand how MidScene is applied.

You can install it directly from the Chrome Web Store Midscene Extension

Configuring the Large Model

After enabling the extension, you need to configure the large model to use. Here we use the Alibaba Qwen multimodal model qwen-vl-max-latest, which consumes relatively few tokens; you can apply for the corresponding API Key through the Alibaba Cloud Bailian platform, and applications currently come with a free quota of 1 million tokens.

After the application is complete, configure the corresponding large model parameters in the extension’s model settings screen; the Qwen model requires the following four parameters

1
2
3

OPENAI_BASE_URL="https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1"
OPENAI_API_KEY="sk- your API KEY"
MIDSCENE_MODEL_NAME="qwen-vl-max-latest"
MIDSCENE_USE_QWEN_VL=1

Operating the Browser

Next you can experience Midscene’s control of the browser in the extension interface. It mainly supports four behaviors:

  • Action: Corresponds to AI-planned operations; Midscene automatically plans the operation steps and executes them. It is smarter but slower, and the results depend on the quality of the large model.
  • Query: Extracts data directly from the UI and, with the reasoning ability of multimodal AI, achieves intelligent extraction
  • Assert: Describes an assertion condition in natural language and lets the AI judge whether the condition is true
  • Tap: Corresponds to an immediate page-click operation; Midscene executes it directly, and the large model only handles low-level tasks such as element locating. It is more efficient and is suitable when the operation to perform is already determined

We can enter prompt instructions using AI prompts close to natural language; for different behavior modes, the extension drives the browser to perform different operations and reports the results.

The concrete execution process can also be seen in the video demo below.

Script Integration

Besides calling Midscene through the browser extension, the more recommended approach is to integrate Midscene capabilities through test framework scripts.

With script integration, you also need to configure the relevant model call parameters, the same variable values configured in the extension, except that the relevant variables need to be set as system environment variables
